evidence_quotes.quote: This paper describes the WaterAid-supported programme of water, sanitation and hygiene education implemented by local NGOs in the “slums” of Bangladesh’s two largest cities, Dhaka and Chittagong.

The evaluation was conducted using a combination of qualitative (observation, group discussions and key informant interviews) and quantitative (household questionnaires) research methods. Approximately half of the 1,130 surveyed households were programme beneficiaries.

As Table 2 demonstrates, more than 98 per cent of beneficiaries have access to supply water (water drawn from the metropolitan authority’s mains) or tubewells within their slums, compared to just over 77 per cent of non-beneficiaries. This represents a 27 per cent overall improvement in access.

As one manager pointed out: “Getting even one legal water point approval from Dhaka Water and Sewerage Authority was impossible six years ago.” Another added: “Gaining any access is the number-one success of this programme.”

The study has found virtually unanimous agreement among the staff and managers of partner NGOs that the programme as organized at present cannot do much for the poorest of the poor. While cost-recovery is manageable for many poor households, it is not for the very poorest.

country.comment: The evaluation examines urban slums in Dhaka and Chittagong, Bangladesh.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title, Summary, and Section I

effect_estimate.comment: Descriptive cross-tabulations from the household survey alongside qualitative evaluation findings; no confidence intervals, standard errors, or p-values are reported in the paper. Note that in Table 3, summing the four high-risk defecation categories for very poor beneficiaries yields 36.5% (28.6% + 1.3% + 2.0% + 4.6%), which the text reports rounded as 37%.
effect_estimate.value: Beneficiary households had higher access to safe drinking water inside their slum (metropolitan authority mains supply or tubewell) than non-beneficiary households: 98.4% (n=491; 45.0% supply inside slum, 53.4% tubewell inside slum) vs. 77.3% (n=639; 43.7% supply inside slum, 33.6% tubewell inside slum), reported as a 27% relative improvement overall, and 98.7% (n=154) vs. 71.5% (n=235) among very poor households (reported as a 38% relative improvement). For sanitation, 37% (36.5% in Table 3) of very poor beneficiary households (n=154) practised high-risk defecation (hang latrines, open spaces, or slabs over drains/water) vs. 54% (54.0% in Table 3) of very poor non-beneficiaries (n=235), and communal latrine use was 31.8% among beneficiaries vs. 19.6% among non-beneficiaries. Institutionally, NGO intermediation secured previously unobtainable legal water point approvals from municipal water authorities (355 water points, tubewells, or sanitation blocks constructed), but full cost-recovery requirements (Tk 60,000 water point loans repaid over 30 months; user fees of Tk 30–35/month or 50 paisa per 20-litre pot = Tk 106–107/month for full 4-person household needs; one NGO abandoned monthly billing at 90% of water points due to non-payment) rationed or excluded the poorest households (incomes <Tk 300–500/month) and limited their participation on facility committees (very poor comprised 21% of committee members overall and 12% on water point committees vs. 55% and 65% for solvent households, n=87). No confidence intervals or p-values reported.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 2 (mechanism directly observed empirically, which is also the design ceiling for a mixed-methods study appraised with MMAT). The study directly documents NGO negotiation of legal municipal water connections, full cost-recovery tariff/loan repayment rules rationing or excluding the poorest, informal fee reductions/exemptions on cluster latrines, landlord control in rental slums, and socioeconomic barriers to committee participation.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines insecure slum land tenure and landlord property control/eviction threats (ELIGIBILITY: tenure, property); full cost-recovery loan repayment and monthly vs. per-pot tariff structures excluding the poorest (BURDEN: fees); and NGO intermediation to obtain legal municipal water authority approvals, informal reduced-fee accommodations for destitute households on water/cluster latrines, and community management committee governance (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: bureaucratic_assistance, hardship_exception, accommodation, participation).

outcome_flags.comment: Measures legal connections to metropolitan water authority mains (formal_connection), access to safe drinking water sources inside/outside slums (water_access), access to sanitary vs. unhygienic defecation facilities (sanitation_access), rationing of household water volumes to 1–2 pots/day vs. 140–160 litres/day needed for bathing/laundry (service_quantity), and payment burdens/exclusion under monthly and per-pot charges relative to slum household incomes (affordability).

publication_year.comment: Published in Environment & Urbanization, Vol. 15, No. 2, October 2003 (summarizing a November 2001 commissioned external evaluation).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: The evaluation integrates both primary quantitative data (cross-sectional household questionnaire survey of 1,130 beneficiary and non-beneficiary households analyzed descriptively) and primary qualitative data (field observation, group discussions, and in-depth/key informant interviews), matching the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). There is no econometric quasi-experimental design (e.g., DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, or controlled before-after) that would warrant ROBINS-I.
